To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the X-ray ionization of heavy elements is a powerful process for the creation of doubly charged ions and that the doubly charged ions are largely confined to the outer hot layers of the disk, where they can be detected by future observations with the James Webb Space Telescope.
(1) X-rays ionize the heavy elements to the doubly charged ion state and (2) the doubly charged ion population is confined to the hot disk atmosphere.

(i) X-ray irradiated protoplanetary disks are hot, with temperatures in the range 10 ^{4} -10 ^{6} K in the upper layers; (ii) the hot gas is mostly ionized, with a high abundance of doubly charged ions, and (iii) the ionization is confined to the outer regions, where it is produced by X-rays and where the ionization is destroyed by recombination.
In summary, our research is concerned with

a detailed understanding of the chemistry of the gas in protostellar disks, and the results are intended to be used in future observational and theoretical studies of the physical conditions in these disks.

the X-ray ionization of heavy elements is important in T Tauri disk atmospheres, and the doubly charged ions are the dominant species.

the ionization of heavy elements in the disk is dominated by X-ray ionization, which is rapidly quenched by recombination, so that the doubly charged ions are largely confined to the outermost layers of the disk atmosphere.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the doubly charged ions of heavy elements are produced in the outer layers of the disks by X-ray ionization, while in the cooler inner layers the singly charged ions are the most abundant.

we have demonstrated the feasibility of using the doubly charged ions to probe the physical conditions in the outer layers of the disks and the abundances of the most abundant heavy elements in those layers.
the ionization of heavy elements by X-rays in protostellar disks is dominated by the Auger effect.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the X-ray ionization of heavy elements is an important process in the chemistry of the disk atmosphere.

the doubly charged ions of the heavy elements are likely to be confined to the disk atmosphere, and the abundances of the singly charged ions in the disk body depend on the heavy-element abundances, which are not well known.
X-ray ionization of heavy elements in the disk atmosphere can be a major factor determining the ionization of the disk gas and the ionization state of the disk atmosphere.
